title: Lesson 32: Building your first enterprise agent: project setup, end to end
description: The boring decisions that decide whether an agent survives contact with a real codebase: a bounded problem, a repository that communicates, wired tools, a typed state, and entry points a team can actually run.

questions.question: Why should an enterprise agent project start from a problem bounded in one sentence?
options: A one-sentence scope lets the agent run without any tools or permissions at all
A narrow scope removes the need for any test set or a defined success condition
Every downstream choice, tools, permissions, and evals, follows from that boundary
A vague scope is acceptable as long as the underlying model is large and capable enough
questions.explanation: A boundary the agent can state in one sentence determines its tools, its permissions, and its evaluation set, which is why a vague ambition lets scope grow to fill the empty repository.

questions.question: How should an enterprise agent project handle its secrets and environment?
options: Commit the keys directly in the repository so every teammate and tool can find them
Keep secrets in a git-ignored environment file and ship a documented example
Hard-code the keys in the agent source so the model can reference them
Store the keys in the model's system prompt so it can authenticate its tools
questions.explanation: Secrets belong in the environment and out of version control, so the repository keeps a documented example file with no real keys and the environment file is git-ignored.

questions.question: Why start with the framework's in-memory state and move to a durable store only later?
options: It is simple for local runs, but it vanishes on restart and is not shared
It is the only option available until the agent has been deployed to production
A durable store cannot be adopted until the agent has well over a hundred tools
It persists across restarts, so a durable store is never actually needed
questions.explanation: In-memory state is fine for local graphs and tests, but it disappears on restart and is not shared across workers, so a durable store is needed before you rely on resuming a run.
